title_en: Ni Peilu, Wang Ying v. China International Trade Center — dispute over infringement of right to reputation
keywords_en: civil; dispute over right to reputation; first instance; basic people's court; Beijing; natural person; legal person; General Principles of the Civil Law; whether a store has the right to inspect customers' belongings; constituent elements of infringement of right to reputation; supermarket shopping; suspicion of theft; inspection of handbags; personal humiliation; protection of personal dignity; right to reputation; International Trade Center infringement of right to reputation dispute
full_text_en:
Ni Peilu and Wang Ying v. China International Trade Center — dispute over infringement of the right to reputation

Plaintiffs: Ni Peilu, female, 21 years old, residing at Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Plaintiffs: Wang Ying, female, 22 years old, residing at Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Defendant: China International Trade Center.

Legal Representative: Sun Suochang, Chairman of the Board.

Plaintiffs Ni Peilu and Wang Ying initiated a lawsuit before the Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing against the defendant, China International Trade Center (hereinafter referred to as "CWTC"), regarding a dispute over infringement of the right to reputation.

Plaintiffs Ni Peilu and Wang Ying alleged: When the plaintiffs were shopping at the Huilian Supermarket, a subsidiary of the defendant, two male attendants of the defendant suspected that the plaintiffs had stolen goods from the supermarket, and forced the plaintiffs to unbutton their coats and open their handbags for inspection. Such conduct by the defendant's staff insulted the plaintiffs' personal dignity and seriously infringed upon the plaintiffs' right to reputation. Therefore, the plaintiffs requested the court to order the defendant to apologize to the plaintiffs and to compensate them for the mental distress caused.

Defendant CWTC defended: The Huilian Supermarket, a subsidiary of the defendant, has a regulation stating that supermarket staff have the right to inspect bags and packages brought into the store by customers at the cashier's counter. This regulation is posted in the form of a notice at the entrance of the supermarket. When the plaintiffs entered the supermarket to shop, they should be deemed to have voluntarily accepted this regulation. According to the law, the constitutive elements of an act infringing upon the right to reputation require that the infringer commits the infringing act in public, thereby causing a decrease in the public's social evaluation of the injured party. The defendant's staff merely inspected the plaintiffs' handbags inside the supermarket and asked whether they had taken goods without paying. This did not in any way lower the public's social evaluation of the two plaintiffs, and therefore does not constitute an infringement upon the plaintiffs' right to reputation. The belief that their right to reputation had been infringed was merely the plaintiffs' subjective perception, not a fact of this case. Accordingly, the plaintiffs' claims are untenable and should be dismissed.

The Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing found the following facts upon trial: The Huilian Supermarket, a subsidiary of the defendant CWTC, adopts an open-shelf retail method, allowing customers to bring their own bags and packages into the store, and a notice posted at the supermarket entrance states: "In accordance with company instructions, cashiers must check bags (including plastic bags) brought into the store by valued customers. Please open your bag for the cashier to inspect."

At approximately 5:00 p.m. on December 23, 1991, the plaintiffs Ni Peilu and Wang Ying entered the Huilian Supermarket to shop. After pausing to look at the candy counter, they proceeded to other shelves to select a photo frame, paid at the cashier's counter, and exited the supermarket. When the two plaintiffs were about five or six meters outside the entrance, they were called back by stock clerks Fu Bin and Gao Deyong, who had chased them out of the supermarket. Fu and Gao asked: "Miss, have you taken any unpaid items out of the store?" The two plaintiffs replied: "No, we haven't." Fu and Gao did not believe them and continued to press: "Did you take anything? Did you or didn't you?" The two plaintiffs still answered: "No, we did not." Fu and Gao then took the two plaintiffs to the supermarket entrance, pointed to the notice on the wall, and said: "We have the right to inspect your handbags." They then led the two plaintiffs into the supermarket office. There, female employee He Jing also joined in questioning the two plaintiffs. After repeated questioning, plaintiff Ni Peilu began to cry, and plaintiff Wang Ying opened her handbag, unbuttoned her coat, and removed her hat for the three staff members to inspect. The three staff members found nothing belonging to the supermarket, so Fu Bin had to say: "I was told by a customer that you had taken something. Sorry, you may go now." The two plaintiffs wanted to speak to the supermarket manager, but were told: "The manager is not in."

The Chaoyang District People's Court held: Right refers to certain acts that citizens or legal persons may perform and certain interests they may enjoy as conferred by law. When citizens or legal persons perform an act, if there is no legal basis or if it does not conform to legal provisions, they cannot consider themselves entitled to perform such an act. The law has never granted supermarket staff the right to interrogate customers or inspect customers' property. Therefore, the defendant had no right to post a notice requiring customers to open their handbags for inspection by the defendant's staff. Although this notice was posted at the supermarket entrance, because it lacked a legal basis, it is invalid, and customers have the right not to comply with its provisions.

Article 101 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Citizens and legal persons shall enjoy the right to reputation. The personality dignity of citizens shall be protected by law, and it shall be prohibited to harm the reputation of citizens or legal persons by means of insult, defamation, or the like." So-called reputation, with respect to citizens, refers to a certain social evaluation of a citizen's moral character, talent, reputation, credit, and other aspects, formed based on the citizen's work, life, words, and other conduct. So-called personality dignity refers to a citizen's self-awareness and self-evaluation of his or her own social status and social value. The right to reputation conferred by law on citizens is a personality right, which is closely related to the citizen's reputation and personal dignity. The defendant's staff suspected that the two plaintiffs had stolen goods from the supermarket. They should have handled the matter in accordance with legal procedures and submitted it to the legal authorities for investigation and disposition. Instead, without conclusive evidence, they called out to the two plaintiffs in a public place and asked whether they had taken unpaid goods out of the store. Although the question was phrased euphemistically, its derogatory implication was obvious. This question was not only sufficient to cause the two plaintiffs to feel that their social status had been belittled, but also actually affected the social evaluation that should have been accorded to the two plaintiffs' moral character, reputation, credit, and other aspects. Therefore, such questioning had already damaged the reputation of the two plaintiffs. Furthermore, relying on the invalid notice of the supermarket, the defendant's staff claimed that they had the right to inspect the plaintiffs' belongings, took the two plaintiffs into the supermarket, and continued to press them with questions. Under these circumstances, although in form the plaintiffs themselves opened their handbags, unbuttoned their coats, and removed their hats for inspection by the supermarket staff, the substance was that the supermarket staff conducted a search of the customers. Such a search may only be conducted by legally authorized authorities. Therefore, the above-mentioned conduct by the defendant's staff seriously infringed upon the right to reputation lawfully enjoyed by the two plaintiffs. Article 120, paragraph 1, of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides that when a citizen's right to reputation is infringed upon, the citizen has the right to demand cessation of the infringement, elimination of the adverse effects, an apology, and may also demand compensation for losses. The plaintiffs' claims are lawful and should be supported. Article 43 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides: "An enterprise legal person shall bear civil liability for the business activities of its legal representative and other staff." When the defendant's staff committed the tortious acts against the two plaintiffs, they were performing the duties assigned to them by the defendant at their work positions. Therefore, the civil liability for the tort shall be borne by the defendant. After the Chaoyang District People's Court ascertained the facts and clarified the rights and wrongs, the defendant expressed its willingness to apologize to the two plaintiffs and pay RMB 1,000 each as compensation for economic losses and mental distress, requesting the plaintiffs to withdraw the complaint. The two plaintiffs accepted the compensation paid by the defendant, expressed their willingness to settle the matter amicably, and submitted an application for withdrawal of the complaint to the People's Court.

After reviewing the application for withdrawal of the complaint by plaintiffs Ni Peilu and Wang Ying, the Chaoyang District People's Court held that the parties had already reached an amicable settlement, and there was no need for further trial of this case. The plaintiffs' application for withdrawal of the complaint complied with the provisions of Article 131, paragraph 1, of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, on November 18, 1992, the court ruled: The withdrawal of the complaint by plaintiffs Ni Peilu and Wang Ying is permitted.
